pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l01.q: A pericardial effusion has accumulated slowly over three months and now measures 1.4 L, yet the patient walks in complaining only of fullness. Why is he not in shock?
choices: The fibrous pericardium stretches when fluid arrives slowly, so pressure inside the sac stays low
Chronic effusions are protein-poor and therefore do not compress the heart
The left ventricle compensates by raising its ejection fraction above 80 percent
Slow effusions collect outside the fibrous pericardium and never touch the heart
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l01.why: The fibrous bag is stiff acutely but does stretch over weeks, so 1 to 2 L can accumulate slowly while as little as 150 to 200 mL arriving fast kills. Protein content and ejection fraction are irrelevant to the mechanism, and the fluid is inside the sac by definition.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l01.q: You hear an extra low-pitched sound immediately BEFORE S1 in a 68-year-old with 20 years of untreated hypertension. Which sound is it and what does it mean?
choices: A pericardial knock, meaning tamponade
S3, meaning a dilated volume-overloaded ventricle
S4, meaning an atrium pushing against a stiff ventricle
An opening snap, meaning mitral stenosis
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l01.why: S4 sits just before S1 because it is the atrial kick striking a non-compliant ventricle, exactly what long-standing hypertension produces. S3 comes just after S2 and means volume overload; an opening snap follows S2; tamponade gives muffled tones, not an extra pre-systolic sound.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l02.q: A patient in a supraventricular tachycardia at 210 beats per minute develops chest pain despite clean coronary arteries on a prior catheterization. What is the mechanism?
choices: Tachycardia raises systolic pressure and ruptures a plaque
Diastole shortens, and since coronaries fill in diastole, supply falls while demand rises
The coronary ostia close at rates above 180
The fast rate directly damages myocytes by mechanical friction
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l02.why: Coronary filling happens in diastole, and tachycardia cuts diastole first, so supply falls exactly when a fast heart needs more. Mechanical friction is not a mechanism, plaque rupture is not required for demand ischemia, and the ostia do not close.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l02.q: ST elevation is present in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which wall and artery is this?
choices: Inferior wall, right coronary artery
Anterior wall, left anterior descending
Septal wall, left anterior descending
Lateral wall, left circumflex
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l02.why: I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral lead group, supplied by the circumflex. The inferior group is II, III and aVF; the septal group is V1 to V2 and the anterior group V3 to V4, both LAD territory.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l03.q: A patient in atrial fibrillation with a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle drops his blood pressure when the rhythm starts. Which part of the cardiac cycle was lost?
choices: Ejection, which is shortened by the irregular rhythm
Isovolumetric relaxation, which allows the aortic valve to close
The atrial kick, which contributes the last 20 to 30 percent of ventricular filling
Isovolumetric contraction, which generates most of the pressure
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l03.why: Passive filling supplies 70 to 80 percent and the atrial kick the last 20 to 30 percent, and a stiff ventricle depends heavily on that kick. Isovolumetric phases move no blood, and ejection is a consequence of filling, not the lost step.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l03.q: A patient has a blood pressure of 100/40 mmHg. Calculate the MAP and decide whether organ autoregulation is protected.
choices: MAP about 60, below the 65 mmHg floor
MAP about 80, comfortably normal
MAP about 50, requiring immediate pressors
MAP about 70, above the 65 mmHg floor
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l03.why: MAP = DBP + 1/3(SBP - DBP) = 40 + 1/3(60) = 60 mmHg, just under the 65 mmHg floor where kidney, brain and gut lose autoregulation. Averaging 100 and 40 to get 70 is the common error; diastole is weighted more because it occupies two-thirds of the cycle.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l04.q: A patient's ECG shows a regular rhythm at 32 beats per minute with no visible P waves and a QRS of 150 ms. Which pacemaker is driving the heart?
choices: An accessory pathway
The SA node at a depressed rate
The AV junction at its intrinsic rate
A ventricular or Purkinje escape focus
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l04.why: A rate of 20 to 40 with a wide QRS and absent P waves is a ventricular escape rhythm, meaning both the SA node and the junction have failed. A junctional escape would be 40 to 60 with a narrow QRS, and a depressed SA node would still produce P waves.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l04.q: Which phase of the ventricular action potential does a calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem principally affect, and what is the bedside consequence?
choices: Phase 0, widening the QRS
Phase 2, reducing contractility and slowing AV nodal conduction
Phase 3, prolonging the QT interval
Phase 4, abolishing the resting potential
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l04.why: Phase 2 is the calcium plateau that triggers contraction, and the AV node depends on calcium current, so diltiazem slows rate and drops contractility, which is why it is risky in a failing ventricle. Phase 0 is sodium, phase 3 is potassium efflux, and phase 4 is maintained by the sodium-potassium ATPase.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l05.q: An arteriole constricts so that its radius falls to half its previous value. What happens to resistance through that vessel?
choices: It quadruples
It rises about sixteenfold
It is unchanged because length did not change
It doubles
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l05.why: Resistance varies inversely with the fourth power of radius, so halving the radius multiplies resistance by 2 to the fourth power, which is 16. Doubling and quadrupling correspond to first and second power relationships, which do not apply.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l05.q: A septic patient has waterlogged tissues and an empty intravascular space. Why does giving albumin fail to pull the fluid back?
choices: Sepsis destroys albumin within minutes of infusion
Hydrostatic pressure in sepsis is too high for any oncotic force to overcome
Albumin is too large to enter the vascular space when given intravenously
The capillary wall is leaking protein, so oncotic pressure equalizes across it
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l05.why: Sepsis raises capillary permeability, so infused protein crosses the wall and the oncotic gradient that would hold water in disappears. Albumin is infused directly into the vasculature and is not instantly destroyed, and hydrostatic pressure in septic shock is typically low, not high.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l06.q: A patient on metoprolol has lost 1.5 L of blood. His heart rate is 78 and blood pressure 104/78. Why is this more worrying than the same numbers in an unmedicated patient?
choices: Beta blockade blocks the baroreflex tachycardia, so the usual early warning sign is absent
Beta blockade increases the rate of bleeding
Beta blockade raises SVR so much that the pressure is falsely elevated
Beta blockade prevents aldosterone release and causes rapid sodium loss
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l06.why: The baroreflex answer to hypovolemia is beta-1 mediated tachycardia, and blocking it removes the first vital sign to change, so these patients crash without the usual warning. Beta blockers do not increase bleeding rate, and the narrow pulse pressure here is the reflex working on the alpha side, not a falsely high reading.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l06.q: A patient develops lip and tongue swelling three weeks after starting lisinopril. Which molecule accumulates to cause this, and what is the reasonable substitute class?
choices: Renin accumulates; substitute a thiazide
Angiotensin II accumulates; substitute a beta blocker
Bradykinin accumulates; substitute an angiotensin receptor blocker
Aldosterone accumulates; substitute spironolactone
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l06.why: ACE also degrades bradykinin, so inhibiting it lets bradykinin build up and cause cough and angioedema; ARBs block the receptor downstream and skip that pathway. ACE inhibitors lower angiotensin II and aldosterone rather than raising them.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l07.q: A 22-year-old is hypotensive with a heart rate of 52, warm dry pink skin and no external bleeding after a diving accident. What is the shock state, and what must still be excluded?
choices: Cardiogenic shock; tamponade must still be excluded
Anaphylactic shock; airway swelling must still be excluded
Obstructive shock; tension pneumothorax must still be excluded
Neurogenic shock; hemorrhage must still be excluded
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l07.why: Hypotension with bradycardia and warm dry skin is the fingerprint of neurogenic shock from a cord injury above roughly T6, which cuts sympathetic outflow. Trauma patients can bleed at the same time, so hemorrhage is still ruled out; cardiogenic and obstructive shock would give cool clamped skin and tachycardia.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l07.q: A septic patient's lactate falls from 6.2 to 5.4 mmol/L after resuscitation. How should this be read?
choices: Excellent clearance, resuscitation can stop
A fall of only about 13 percent, short of the 10 to 20 percent target for clearance and still over 4 mmol/L, so hypoperfusion persists
Lactate is unreliable in sepsis and should be ignored
The value is now normal since normal is under 6 mmol/L
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l07.why: Normal lactate is under 2 mmol/L and over 4 marks severe hypoperfusion, so 5.4 is still abnormal even though the trend has begun to move. Serial lactate is more informative than a single value, and a 10 to 20 percent clearance is the target, not a signal to stop.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l08.q: A 70 kg patient is ventilated at a tidal volume of 450 mL and a rate of 12. Approximately what is the alveolar ventilation?
choices: 7.2 L/min
5.4 L/min
3.6 L/min
1.8 L/min
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l08.why: Anatomic dead space is about 2 mL/kg, so 140 to 150 mL here; (450 - 150) x 12 is about 3.6 L/min. The 5.4 L/min figure is minute ventilation, which counts the dead space that clears no CO2.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l08.q: A patient with a right middle lobe pneumonia has a completely clear posterior lung exam. Why?
choices: The right middle lobe projects anteriorly and laterally at the fourth to sixth spaces and reaches no posterior surface
The right middle lobe is behind the heart and produces no sound anywhere
Posterior auscultation only detects upper lobes at any level
Right middle lobe consolidation resolves before physical signs appear
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l08.why: The right middle lobe sits anteriorly and laterally between the horizontal and oblique fissures and has no posterior surface, so listening on the back misses it entirely. Posterior listening below the scapular spine picks up lower lobes, and consolidation does not vanish from the exam before it resolves.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l09.q: A patient's SpO2 falls from 94 to 88 percent. Why is that six-point fall more alarming than a fall from 100 to 94 percent?
choices: Because 90 percent corresponds to PaO2 60 mmHg, the cliff edge of the curve, so below it PaO2 falls steeply for each point lost
Because saturation and PaO2 are linearly related throughout the range
Because 88 percent is the arbitrary threshold for oxygen therapy
Because pulse oximetry is inaccurate above 94 percent
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l09.why: The oxyhemoglobin curve is flat above roughly PaO2 60 (SpO2 90) and steep below it, so points lost below 90 represent much larger PaO2 drops. The relationship is sigmoid, not linear, and oximetry is reasonably accurate in the high range.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l09.q: Why do fibrosis and pulmonary edema cause hypoxemia well before they cause CO2 retention?
choices: The body suppresses CO2 production when the membrane thickens
Hemoglobin buffers CO2 completely up to a PaCO2 of 80
CO2 diffuses about 20 times more readily than oxygen, so a thickened membrane limits oxygen first
CO2 is carried entirely dissolved and is unaffected by membranes
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l09.why: The higher solubility of CO2 makes it about 20 times more diffusible than oxygen, so a thickened alveolar-capillary barrier restricts oxygen transfer long before CO2 transfer. Most CO2 travels as bicarbonate rather than dissolved, and production is not suppressed on demand.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l10.q: Interpret: pH 7.48, PaCO2 28 mmHg, HCO3 21 mEq/L in an anxious patient with sudden pleuritic chest pain.
choices: Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Respiratory alkalosis with early metabolic compensation
Fully compensated metabolic acidosis
Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l10.why: The pH is alkalemic and the low PaCO2 moves in the same direction as the pH, so the respiratory side is primary; the slightly low bicarbonate is the kidney beginning to compensate. A metabolic alkalosis would have a high bicarbonate, and respiratory acidosis would show a high PaCO2 with a low pH.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l10.q: A COPD patient arrives with SpO2 78 percent. What is the correct oxygen strategy and why?
choices: Give 15 L by non-rebreather and target 100 percent
Give oxygen only after an arterial blood gas confirms the PaCO2
Withhold oxygen to preserve hypoxic drive
Give oxygen titrated to SpO2 88 to 92 percent and monitor mental status
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l10.why: Hypoxia kills faster than hypercapnia, so oxygen is given but titrated to 88 to 92 percent; the risk of over-oxygenation is worsened V/Q matching from lost hypoxic vasoconstriction plus the Haldane effect, not simple drive suppression. Withholding oxygen and waiting for a gas both leave the patient hypoxic, and targeting 100 percent invites retention.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l11.q: An 80-year-old with known aortic stenosis has chest pain and is given sublingual nitroglycerin. His systolic pressure falls from 128 to 74 mmHg. What is the mechanism?
choices: Nitroglycerin directly poisons the hypertrophied myocardium
Nitroglycerin caused reflex bradycardia and reduced cardiac output
The fixed valve orifice prevents stroke volume from rising, so a preload drop cannot be compensated
Nitroglycerin dilates the stenotic valve and causes acute regurgitation
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l11.why: Severe aortic stenosis is preload dependent because a fixed orifice caps stroke volume, so venodilation drops output with nothing available to compensate. Nitroglycerin does not dilate valves, and reflex tachycardia rather than bradycardia is the usual response.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l11.q: Which finding distinguishes ACUTE aortic regurgitation from the chronic form at the bedside?
choices: A narrow pulse pressure with tachycardia and pulmonary edema
A mid-systolic click
A wide pulse pressure with a bounding collapsing pulse
A loud long decrescendo murmur
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l11.why: In acute regurgitation the ventricle has had no time to dilate, so the pulse pressure stays narrow and the patient is tachycardic and in flash edema; the murmur is short and soft. Wide pulse pressure and a loud long murmur belong to the chronic form, and a click belongs to mitral valve prolapse.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l12.q: A patient with mitral stenosis has an S2-to-opening-snap interval that has shortened compared with a recording from two years ago. What does that mean?
choices: The stenosis has improved
The patient has developed aortic regurgitation
The finding is a measurement artifact with no meaning
The stenosis has worsened and left atrial pressure is higher
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l12.why: A higher left atrial pressure forces the mitral valve open sooner after S2, so a shorter interval means more severe stenosis. A longer interval would suggest milder disease, and the interval is a recognized severity marker rather than an artifact.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l12.q: A patient with a mechanical mitral valve reports two weeks of increasing dyspnea, and the crisp metallic click you documented last year is now muffled. What is the concern?
choices: Normal valve aging with no clinical significance
Prosthetic valve thrombosis, an emergency
Development of an innocent flow murmur
Pericardial friction rub obscuring the click
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l12.why: A mechanical valve should click crisply, and a muffled or absent click with new symptoms suggests valve thrombosis, which is a surgical or thrombolytic emergency. Mechanical valves do not lose their click with age, and a rub is scratchy and does not silence a metallic click.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l13.q: A patient has 3 mm of concave ST elevation in nearly every lead, PR depression, and no reciprocal ST depression except in aVR. What is the diagnosis and what argues against occlusion?
choices: Anterolateral STEMI; the diffuse distribution confirms a large infarct
Pericarditis; diffuse concave elevation with PR depression and absent reciprocal change
Left ventricular hypertrophy with strain; the concavity is diagnostic
Hyperkalemia; PR depression is the earliest sign
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l13.why: Diffuse concave elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change outside aVR is pericarditis; a true occlusion respects a territory and brings reciprocal depression. Hypertrophy with strain gives ST depression laterally, and hyperkalemia begins with peaked T waves.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l13.q: Which ECG finding indicates left atrial enlargement, and which valve lesion classically produces it?
choices: An R wave taller than the S in V1; mitral regurgitation
S in V1 plus R in V5 over 35 mm; aortic stenosis
A peaked P wave over 2.5 mm in lead II; tricuspid stenosis
A wide notched P wave in lead II; mitral stenosis
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l13.why: P mitrale, a wide notched P in lead II, marks left atrial enlargement and accompanies mitral stenosis, where the obstruction sits upstream of the ventricle. P pulmonale, the tall peaked P, is right atrial; the V1 R/S ratio marks right ventricular hypertrophy and the 35 mm sum marks left ventricular hypertrophy.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l14.q: A patient's FEV1 is 1.60 L and FVC is 2.00 L. What is the ratio and what does it indicate?
choices: 0.80, indicating a non-obstructive pattern that may be restrictive
1.25, an invalid result
0.62, indicating obstruction
0.80, indicating obstruction
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l14.why: 1.60 divided by 2.00 is 0.80, above the 0.70 threshold, so obstruction is excluded; with a reduced FVC the pattern suggests restriction, which must be confirmed with a total lung capacity under 80 percent predicted. The ratio cannot exceed 1 because FEV1 is part of FVC.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l14.q: A patient's flow-volume loop shows flattening of BOTH the inspiratory and expiratory limbs. What does this indicate?
choices: Emphysema with small airway collapse
Interstitial fibrosis
Fixed upper airway obstruction such as tracheal stenosis
Vocal cord dysfunction
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l14.why: A fixed lesion limits flow equally in both directions and flattens both limbs; a variable extrathoracic lesion such as vocal cord dysfunction flattens only the inspiratory limb. Emphysema scoops the expiratory limb, and fibrosis produces a narrow tall loop at low volumes.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l15.q: A patient in pressure control ventilation has a tidal volume that has drifted from 480 mL down to 300 mL at unchanged settings. What has happened?
choices: The ventilator has silently switched to volume control
The set rate has increased
The patient's compliance has improved
The patient's compliance has worsened, so the set pressure now moves less volume
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l15.why: Pressure modes guarantee pressure and let volume vary, so a falling tidal volume at fixed pressure means stiffer lungs or higher resistance. Improved compliance would raise the delivered volume, and the rate does not change tidal volume.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l15.q: Which combination of ventilator settings is correct for an intubated status asthmaticus patient?
choices: Rate 24, I:E 1:1, targeting a normal PaCO2
Rate 8 to 10, I:E 1:4 to 1:5, accepting a high PaCO2 while pH stays above about 7.20
Rate 16, PEEP 15, targeting a plateau pressure of 35
Rate 20 with tidal volumes of 12 mL/kg to force air out
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l15.why: Obstructed patients cannot exhale fully, so the rate is slowed and expiratory time lengthened, and permissive hypercapnia is accepted down to a pH of about 7.20. Fast rates, short expiratory times and large tidal volumes all stack air and cause hypotension, and a plateau over 30 injures lung.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l16.q: An upright chest film in a patient with heart failure looks normal, but bedside ultrasound shows a clear anechoic stripe above the diaphragm. How much fluid does each test need to detect?
choices: Ultrasound cannot quantify pleural fluid at all
Film about 50 mL, ultrasound about 500 mL
Film 200 to 500 mL, ultrasound about 50 mL
Both detect about 200 mL
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l16.why: An upright film needs roughly 200 to 500 mL before the costophrenic angle blunts, while ultrasound detects about 50 mL, which is why it has largely replaced the film for this question. A supine film is even less sensitive and just makes the hemithorax hazy.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l16.q: Why is needle decompression at the fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line often preferred over the second space in adults?
choices: The chest wall is thinner there, so a standard catheter is more likely to reach the pleural space
It avoids the risk of pneumothorax
It is the only site that also drains blood
The pleural space is larger there
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l16.why: Chest wall thickness at the second intercostal space frequently exceeds standard catheter length, and the lateral site is thinner, so decompression succeeds more often. The procedure is being performed in a pneumothorax already, and a chest tube follows at either site.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l17.q: Why does a large fluid bolus often worsen a patient with acute right ventricular failure?
choices: It overdistends the right ventricle and worsens septal bowing into the left ventricle
It raises systemic vascular resistance sharply
It causes reflex bradycardia
It dilutes clotting factors and causes bleeding
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l17.why: An already dilated right ventricle pushes the septum leftward when it is overfilled, further impairing left ventricular filling and dropping output, which is why boluses are given 250 mL at a time. Dilution and reflex bradycardia are not the operative mechanisms, and fluid does not raise SVR.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l17.q: Which pulmonary hypertension group is most common, and why does misclassifying it matter?
choices: Group 5; no treatment exists for any group
Group 1; pulmonary vasodilators are withheld unnecessarily
Group 2 from left heart disease; pulmonary vasodilators can flood a left ventricle that cannot keep up
Group 4; anticoagulation would be missed
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l17.why: Group 2 from left heart disease is by far the most common, and lowering pulmonary resistance sends more blood to a left ventricle that already cannot handle it, causing pulmonary edema. Group 4 is the potentially curable thromboembolic group, and group 1 is the one that actually receives targeted vasodilators.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l18.q: A newborn passes the right hand pulse oximetry reading at 97 percent but the foot reads 91 percent. How is the screen interpreted?
choices: Passed, because the right hand is above 95 percent
Failed, because the pre- and post-ductal difference exceeds 3 percent and the foot is under 95 percent
Indeterminate, requiring a repeat in one week
Failed only if both readings are under 90 percent
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l18.why: A failed screen is a saturation under 95 percent in either limb or a pre- to post-ductal difference over 3 percent; here both criteria are met, which points toward a ductal-dependent lesion. A single normal reading does not pass the screen, and the evaluation is not deferred a week.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l18.q: A 5-year-old has a soft grade 2 systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border that softens when she sits up, with a normally splitting S2 and normal growth. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: A ventricular septal defect requiring urgent echocardiography
An atrial septal defect, because the murmur is at the pulmonic area
Aortic stenosis, because it is systolic
An innocent murmur; no further workup needed on these features
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l18.why: Soft, grade 2 or less, systolic only, position-variable, with a normally splitting S2 in a well child is the innocent profile. An atrial septal defect gives a wide fixed split S2, a ventricular septal defect gives a harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower sternal border, and aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l19.q: During maximal exercise, which variable carries the increase in cardiac output once effort exceeds roughly half of maximum?
choices: Hemoglobin concentration, which rises acutely
Stroke volume, which keeps rising to the end
Heart rate, because stroke volume has already plateaued
Systemic vascular resistance, which rises to boost pressure
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l19.why: Stroke volume rises about 50 percent and then plateaus at roughly 40 to 60 percent of maximal effort, so further output comes from rate, which is why maximal heart rate sets the ceiling. Resistance falls as muscle arterioles dilate, and hemoglobin does not rise acutely in any meaningful way.

pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l19.q: A 27-year-old non-smoker has emphysema predominantly at the lung BASES and abnormal liver enzymes. What should be tested?
choices: Alpha-1 antitrypsin level
Carboxyhemoglobin by co-oximetry
Vitamin E acetate in a vape cartridge
Sweat chloride for cystic fibrosis
pa-anatomy-cardio-resp-l19.why: Basilar emphysema in a young non-smoker with liver disease is the alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency pattern, an unopposed protease problem. Smoking-related emphysema is apical, EVALI presents acutely with ground-glass opacities, and cystic fibrosis gives bronchiectasis rather than basilar emphysema with hepatitis.

quiz.q: A 30-year-old is stabbed in the chest and arrives with BP 82/66, HR 134, distended neck veins and clear equal breath sounds. A 500 mL crystalloid bolus raises the systolic to 96 for four minutes, then it falls again. What does the transient response tell you?
choices: Volume briefly raised filling pressure above the pericardial pressure, but the sac is still full, so drainage is the definitive fix
The response proves hypovolemic rather than obstructive shock
The patient needs a diuretic to reduce the elevated venous pressure
The bleeding has stopped and no further intervention is needed
quiz.why: In tamponade a bolus can briefly overcome the pressure in the sac and buy minutes, but only drainage fixes it. A transient response does not exclude tamponade; hypovolemic shock would show flat neck veins, and a diuretic lowers the preload the compressed heart depends on.

quiz.q: Which structure prevents the mitral valve leaflets from inverting into the left atrium during ventricular contraction?
choices: The fibrous pericardium
The endocardial lining of the atrium
The chordae tendineae anchored to the papillary muscles
The three cusps filling with back-pressure
quiz.why: The atrioventricular valves are tethered by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles, which hold the leaflets in place against ventricular pressure. The cup-filling mechanism belongs to the semilunar valves, which have no chordae, and the pericardium and endocardium play no role in leaflet position.

quiz.q: A patient with pericarditis has ST elevation in leads I, II, III, aVF, and V2 through V6. Why is this pattern inconsistent with a single coronary occlusion?
choices: Because ST elevation never occurs in pericarditis
Because the elevation crosses several vascular territories at once, which no single artery supplies
Because pericarditis involves only the endocardium
Because occlusions produce ST depression, not elevation
quiz.why: Pericarditis inflames the sac surrounding the whole heart, so elevation appears across territories, while an occlusion respects the wall its artery feeds. Pericarditis characteristically does cause ST elevation, it involves the pericardium rather than endocardium, and full-thickness occlusion produces elevation.

quiz.q: A 62-year-old with an inferior STEMI develops complete heart block with a junctional escape at 42. Which anatomic fact explains this complication?
choices: The AV node has no dedicated blood supply
The LAD supplies the AV node in most people
The circumflex supplies the bundle of His in most people
The RCA supplies the AV node in about 85 to 90 percent of people
quiz.why: The same RCA that feeds the inferior wall supplies the AV node in 85 to 90 percent of people, so inferior infarcts commonly bring bradycardia and block. The LAD supplies the bundle branch system rather than the node, and the node is definitely perfused.

quiz.q: During cardiac arrest, why do frequent interruptions in chest compressions rapidly reduce the chance of return of spontaneous circulation?
choices: Pausing raises the aortic diastolic pressure above safe limits
Compression pauses cause immediate hyperkalemia
Coronary perfusion pressure falls to near zero within seconds and must be rebuilt with repeated compressions
Interruptions allow the myocardium to cool below its working temperature
quiz.why: Coronary perfusion pressure is aortic diastolic pressure minus left ventricular end-diastolic pressure, and it collapses within seconds of stopping compressions, taking several compressions to rebuild. Cooling, hyperkalemia and excessive diastolic pressure are not the mechanisms.

quiz.q: Tall R waves with ST depression in V1 to V3 accompany ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which artery is most likely responsible?
choices: Left circumflex
Right ventricular branch
Left main only
Left anterior descending
quiz.why: The lateral elevation plus a posterior mirror image points to the circumflex, which supplies the lateral wall and the posterior wall in left-dominant people. The LAD supplies anterior and septal walls, and a left main lesion typically gives diffuse depression with aVR elevation.

quiz.q: A ventricle with an end-diastolic volume of 180 mL ejects 54 mL per beat at a heart rate of 95. What are the ejection fraction and cardiac output?
choices: EF 54 percent, CO about 5.1 L/min
EF 30 percent, CO about 17 L/min
EF 70 percent, CO about 3.4 L/min
EF 30 percent, CO about 5.1 L/min
quiz.why: EF is 54/180 = 30 percent, and CO is 54 mL x 95 = about 5.1 L/min, showing how a badly reduced EF can still deliver a near-normal output. Confusing stroke volume with a percentage or multiplying end-diastolic volume by rate produces the other answers.

quiz.q: Which change increases myocardial oxygen consumption the most for a given cardiac output?
choices: Reducing afterload with a vasodilator
Raising heart rate from 70 to 140
Lowering contractility with a beta blocker
Reducing preload with a nitrate
quiz.why: Doubling the rate doubles the number of isovolumetric contractions, the phase where most oxygen is consumed, while also cutting diastolic perfusion time. Lowering afterload, contractility and preload all reduce myocardial oxygen demand.

quiz.q: A patient's blood pressure reads 88/44 mmHg. Which statement about perfusion is most accurate?
choices: MAP is about 66, just above the autoregulation floor of 65 mmHg
MAP is about 59, below the floor, so organ flow begins to track pressure directly
MAP is 66 and therefore the patient is normotensive
MAP cannot be estimated from a cuff reading
quiz.why: MAP = 44 + 1/3(44) = about 59 mmHg, under the 65 mmHg floor where kidney, brain and gut lose autoregulation. Simply averaging the two numbers overestimates MAP because diastole occupies two-thirds of the cycle, and cuff-based estimation is standard practice.

quiz.q: A patient with a serum potassium of 2.6 mEq/L has a flattened T wave, a prominent U wave and a long QT. Which arrhythmia is he at greatest risk for?
choices: Complete heart block
Atrial flutter
Sinus arrest
Torsades de pointes
quiz.why: Hypokalemia prolongs repolarization, produces U waves, and predisposes to torsades de pointes. Complete heart block, flutter and sinus arrest are not the characteristic consequences of low potassium in this pattern.

quiz.q: Why can cardiac muscle not be tetanized the way skeletal muscle can?
choices: The long phase 2 calcium plateau keeps the cell refractory through most of the contraction
Cardiac muscle has no sarcoplasmic reticulum
The SA node fires too slowly to summate
Cardiac muscle lacks actin and myosin
quiz.why: The plateau extends the refractory period across nearly the whole contraction, so a second stimulus cannot summate. Cardiac muscle does have actin, myosin and a sarcoplasmic reticulum, and pacemaker rate is not the limiting factor.

quiz.q: A missed-dialysis patient has a potassium of 7.4 mEq/L with a QRS of 140 ms. He receives calcium gluconate and the QRS narrows within two minutes, but a repeat potassium is still 7.3. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: The narrowed QRS means the hyperkalemia has resolved
The laboratory result must be erroneous
Calcium stabilizes the myocyte membrane without lowering serum potassium, so shifting and removal therapies are still required
Calcium works slowly and the potassium will fall over the next hour
quiz.why: Calcium raises the threshold potential and protects the membrane within minutes but removes no potassium, so insulin with glucose, albuterol and definitive removal such as dialysis must follow. A narrower QRS reflects membrane stabilization, not a corrected level.

quiz.q: A woman develops arm swelling two years after axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer. Which Starling mechanism explains the edema?
choices: Increased capillary permeability from inflammation
Raised capillary hydrostatic pressure
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure
Blocked lymphatic drainage of the 2 to 4 L filtered daily
quiz.why: Node dissection interrupts the lymphatics that normally return the 2 to 4 L filtered each day, so protein-rich fluid accumulates. Her albumin and capillary pressure are normal, and there is no acute inflammatory leak in chronic lymphedema.

quiz.q: At the venous end of a capillary, hydrostatic pressure is about 15 mmHg and oncotic pressure about 25 mmHg. What is the net effect?
choices: Protein moves out of the capillary
Fluid is reabsorbed into the capillary
Fluid continues to filter out into the interstitium
There is no net movement at any point
quiz.why: At the venous end oncotic pull of about 25 mmHg exceeds hydrostatic push of about 15 mmHg, so fluid returns to the capillary. Filtration dominates at the arterial end where hydrostatic pressure is about 35 mmHg, and protein does not normally cross a healthy wall.

quiz.q: A patient placed on prolonged bed rest develops a calf deep vein thrombosis. Which normal mechanism of venous return was lost?
choices: Capillary oncotic pressure
Arterial elastic recoil
The skeletal muscle pump acting with one-way venous valves
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction
quiz.why: Calf contraction squeezing veins against one-way valves is a major driver of venous return, and immobility removes it, producing the stasis leg of Virchow's triad. Arterial recoil maintains forward arterial flow, and the other two options have nothing to do with venous return.

quiz.q: Which combination correctly describes the actions of angiotensin II?
choices: Arteriolar constriction, aldosterone release, thirst, and ADH release
Bradykinin degradation and potassium retention
Sodium excretion and vasodilation at the kidney
Arteriolar dilation, aldosterone suppression, and diuresis
quiz.why: Angiotensin II raises pressure by constricting arterioles and by expanding volume through aldosterone, thirst and ADH. Sodium excretion and vasodilation describe the natriuretic peptides, which oppose RAAS, and bradykinin degradation is a function of ACE itself.

quiz.q: A dyspneic 80-year-old with chronic kidney disease has a BNP of 260 pg/mL. How should this be used?
choices: It is an intermediate value in a patient whose age and kidney disease independently raise BNP, so it is one input rather than a verdict
BNP is invalid in anyone over 70
It confirms acute heart failure
It excludes acute heart failure
quiz.why: Values under about 100 pg/mL argue against acute heart failure and values over 400 to 500 support it, leaving 260 in between, and both advanced age and renal failure raise BNP independently. It remains a usable but non-diagnostic input at any age.

quiz.q: Which drug spares potassium because it blocks the mineralocorticoid receptor rather than an earlier step in RAAS?
choices: Metoprolol
Losartan
Spironolactone
Lisinopril
quiz.why: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone at its receptor, so the distal nephron stops trading potassium for sodium. Losartan blocks the angiotensin II receptor, lisinopril blocks the converting enzyme, and metoprolol reduces renin release, all upstream of the aldosterone receptor.

quiz.q: A patient after a large anterior MI has BP 84/60, HR 112, distended neck veins, crackles to both mid-fields and cool mottled skin. Which term of MAP = CO x SVR has failed, and what is the expected SVR?
choices: Heart rate has failed and SVR is normal
Contractility has failed and SVR is high as a compensatory response
SVR has failed and contractility is normal
Preload has failed and SVR is low
quiz.why: Hypotension with distended neck veins and pulmonary crackles is cardiogenic shock: the pump has failed while the reflex raises SVR, producing cool mottled skin. Distributive shock would give warm skin with low SVR, and hypovolemia would give flat neck veins and clear lungs.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old after a motorcycle crash has BP 118/76, HR 126, capillary refill 4 seconds, anxiety and a urine output of 15 mL over the last hour in a 70 kg body. What stage of shock is this?
choices: Decompensated shock
Irreversible shock
No shock, since the blood pressure is normal
Compensated shock
quiz.why: Tachycardia, delayed refill, anxiety and urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h with a preserved blood pressure is compensated shock, the stage that is cheap to fix and easy to miss. Decompensation is marked by hypotension and dulled mentation, and a normal pressure never excludes shock.

quiz.q: Which shock state is characterized by normal or elevated preload with a mechanical barrier to flow despite a normal pump and normal blood volume?
choices: Neurogenic shock
Distributive shock
Obstructive shock
Hypovolemic shock
quiz.why: Obstructive shock covers tension pneumothorax, tamponade and massive pulmonary embolism, where the circuit is physically blocked even though the heart muscle and blood volume are intact. Hypovolemic shock lacks volume, distributive shock lacks resistance, and neurogenic shock is a subtype of distributive.

quiz.q: A 60 kg patient breathes at a rate of 20 with a tidal volume of 400 mL. Approximately what fraction of each breath reaches alveoli?
choices: About 70 percent, since dead space is about 120 mL
About 50 percent, since dead space is about 200 mL
100 percent, since dead space applies only to ventilated patients
About 30 percent, since dead space is about 280 mL
quiz.why: Anatomic dead space is about 2 mL/kg, so 120 mL here, leaving 280 of 400 mL, roughly 70 percent, reaching alveoli. Dead space exists in every spontaneous breath, and it scales with body size rather than being a fixed large fraction.

quiz.q: Which pair correctly matches a disease to the mechanical property it changes?
choices: Pulmonary edema raises compliance; COPD reduces it
Neither compliance nor resistance changes in obstructive disease
Asthma reduces compliance; fibrosis raises resistance
Emphysema raises compliance abnormally; ARDS reduces compliance
quiz.why: Emphysema destroys elastic tissue so the lung fills easily and empties poorly, while ARDS, fibrosis and edema stiffen the lung and reduce compliance. Asthma raises resistance rather than reducing compliance, and pulmonary edema reduces compliance.

quiz.q: A patient with a cervical spinal cord injury at C2 is apneic while a patient injured at C6 breathes with the diaphragm but cannot cough forcefully. What explains the difference?
choices: C6 injuries always require ventilation and C2 injuries never do
The phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5, so a C2 lesion denervates the diaphragm while a C6 lesion spares it but takes the intercostals and abdominals
The phrenic nerve arises from C6 to C8
The diaphragm is innervated by the vagus nerve
quiz.why: C3, C4 and C5 keep the diaphragm alive, so a lesion above C3 stops breathing while a lower cervical lesion preserves diaphragmatic breathing but removes the intercostal and abdominal muscles needed for a forceful cough. The vagus does not drive the diaphragm.

quiz.q: A patient with a hemoglobin of 7.0 g/dL has an SpO2 of 100 percent, while another with a hemoglobin of 14.0 g/dL has an SpO2 of 88 percent. Which carries more oxygen per deciliter of blood?
choices: The first patient, because saturation is higher
The second patient, because content depends on hemoglobin mass times saturation
They are equal because both have adequate PaO2
Neither, because oxygen content is determined by dissolved oxygen
quiz.why: Each gram of hemoglobin binds up to 1.34 mL of oxygen, so 14 x 0.88 far exceeds 7 x 1.00; saturation is a percentage of the seats filled, not the number of seats. Only about 2 percent of oxygen travels dissolved, so PaO2 alone does not determine content.

quiz.q: Why does chronic hypoxia from advanced COPD lead to right heart failure?
choices: Hypoxia causes systemic vasodilation and volume overload of the right heart
Hypoxia destroys the tricuspid valve
Hypoxia directly weakens right ventricular myocytes
Global hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction raises pulmonary vascular resistance, and the right ventricle fails against the load
quiz.why: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction is protective when local but becomes a global afterload problem in diffuse lung disease, producing pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale. It does not act by direct myocyte toxicity, systemic vasodilation or valve destruction.

quiz.q: Which condition shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the LEFT?
choices: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Vigorous exercise raising 2,3-DPG
Fever of 39.8 C
Acidosis with a pH of 7.18
quiz.why: Carbon monoxide both occupies binding sites and shifts the curve left, so the remaining oxygen is held more tightly and released less at tissue. Heat, acid, DPG and exercise are the CADET conditions that shift the curve right.

quiz.q: Interpret: pH 7.51, PaCO2 48 mmHg, HCO3 37 mEq/L in a patient with three days of vomiting.
choices: Fully compensated respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
Metabolic alkalosis with partial respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with a raised anion gap
quiz.why: The pH is alkalemic and the raised bicarbonate moves in the same direction as the pH, so the metabolic side is primary; the elevated PaCO2 is hypoventilation compensating. Respiratory alkalosis would show a low PaCO2, and an acidosis would show a pH under 7.35.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old has a PaO2 of 54 mmHg and a PaCO2 of 39 mmHg. His calculated A-a gradient is 38. What does this indicate?
choices: A normal gradient indicating altitude exposure
Laboratory error, since a gradient cannot exceed 20
Hypoventilation, since the gradient is normal for his age
A widened gradient indicating a lung problem such as pneumonia, edema, embolism or shunt
quiz.why: A normal gradient is roughly age/4 + 4, about 19 at 60, so 38 is clearly widened and points at the lung itself. Hypoventilation and altitude both lower arterial and alveolar oxygen together and leave the gradient normal, and gradients well above 20 are common in disease.

quiz.q: A patient with a large intracerebral hemorrhage has irregular breaths of varying depth separated by irregular pauses. What is the pattern and what does it imply?
choices: Kussmaul breathing compensating for a metabolic acidosis
Biot or ataxic breathing, indicating medullary damage and an ominous prognosis
Agonal gasping requiring immediate CPR
Cheyne-Stokes breathing from delayed feedback in the control loop
quiz.why: Irregular depth with irregular pauses is Biot or ataxic breathing, which localizes to the medulla and carries a poor prognosis. Cheyne-Stokes has a regular crescendo-decrescendo cycle, Kussmaul is deep and regular, and agonal breathing is slow ineffective gasping in a pulseless patient.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old has a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, plus an S3. Which lesion and which chamber change does this describe?
choices: Mitral stenosis with a dilated left atrium only
Tricuspid regurgitation with right ventricular hypertrophy
Chronic mitral regurgitation with a dilated, volume-overloaded left ventricle
Aortic stenosis with a thickened left ventricle
quiz.why: A holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla with an S3 is chronic mitral regurgitation, a volume-overload lesion that dilates the ventricle. Aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids and gives an S4, mitral stenosis is a diastolic rumble, and tricuspid regurgitation is loudest at the lower sternal border and increases with inspiration.

quiz.q: A 46-year-old with a bicuspid aortic valve now has severe aortic stenosis. Compared with calcific degeneration in an 80-year-old, what does the bicuspid valve explain?
choices: The same stenotic process presenting roughly two decades earlier
An absence of left ventricular hypertrophy
Radiation to the axilla rather than the carotids
A murmur that is diastolic rather than systolic
quiz.why: A bicuspid valve carries abnormal shear stress and calcifies far earlier, producing the same picture about twenty years sooner. The murmur, the hypertrophy and the carotid radiation are identical regardless of which mechanism caused the stenosis.

quiz.q: A patient's systolic murmur is loudest while standing and becomes noticeably softer when he squats and grips a handgrip dynamometer. What is the lesion and the mechanism?
choices: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; squatting and handgrip raise preload and afterload, opening the outflow tract
Ventricular septal defect; posture does not affect the shunt
Aortic stenosis; squatting increases flow across the valve
Mitral regurgitation; handgrip reduces regurgitant volume
quiz.why: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy behaves opposite to every other murmur: less preload brings the obstructing structures closer and makes it louder, while squatting and handgrip enlarge the cavity and quiet it. Aortic stenosis and mitral regurgitation both get louder with squatting and handgrip respectively.

quiz.q: Which technique is required to hear an S3 or the rumble of mitral stenosis?
choices: The bell pressed firmly at the left lower sternal border
The diaphragm with the patient sitting forward at end-expiration
The bell pressed lightly at the apex with the patient in the left lateral decubitus position
The diaphragm pressed firmly at the right upper sternal border
quiz.why: These are low-pitched sounds, so the bell is used with light pressure, and rolling the patient left brings the apex against the chest wall. Pressing the bell hard converts it into a diaphragm, and the sitting-forward diaphragm technique is for the high-pitched murmur of aortic regurgitation and for a friction rub.

quiz.q: A patient's S2 is single during inspiration and split during expiration. What does this paradoxical pattern indicate?
choices: Right bundle branch block
Something delaying the left ventricle, such as left bundle branch block or severe aortic stenosis
A normal physiologic split
An atrial septal defect
quiz.why: Paradoxical splitting means aortic closure is delayed past pulmonic closure, so inspiration brings them together instead of apart, and the causes are left-sided delays. An atrial septal defect gives a wide fixed split, right bundle branch block gives a widened but still variable split, and a normal split widens with inspiration.

quiz.q: A patient's jugular venous pressure RISES with inspiration. What is this sign called and what does it suggest?
choices: Pulsus paradoxus, suggesting tamponade
A normal respiratory variation
Pulsus alternans, suggesting severe left ventricular dysfunction
Kussmaul sign, suggesting constrictive pericarditis or right ventricular infarct
quiz.why: Inspiration normally lowers jugular venous pressure by dropping intrathoracic pressure, so a rise is Kussmaul sign and points at constriction or a right ventricular infarct. Pulsus alternans is alternating beat strength, and pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory fall in systolic pressure over 10 mmHg.

quiz.q: A patient with chest pain has upsloping ST depression at the J point across the precordial leads with tall, symmetric, peaked T waves and no ST elevation. What does this represent?
choices: A normal variant in an athlete
Hyperkalemia requiring calcium
The de Winter pattern, treated as an LAD occlusion equivalent
Benign early repolarization
quiz.why: The de Winter pattern identifies an acutely occluded LAD despite failing to meet ST-elevation criteria, and it is managed as an occlusion. Hyperkalemic T waves are narrow-based without the upsloping J point depression, and early repolarization and athletic variants do not carry this combination in a patient with chest pain.

quiz.q: An ECG shows a QTc of 520 ms. Why does this number change management?
choices: Torsades de pointes risk climbs sharply above 500 ms, so QT-prolonging drugs are avoided and magnesium and electrolytes are addressed
It indicates left ventricular hypertrophy
A QTc over 500 ms is normal in women
It confirms hyperkalemia
quiz.why: Normal QTc is under about 440 ms in men and 460 ms in women, and above 500 ms the risk of torsades rises steeply, which drives drug avoidance and electrolyte correction. Hypertrophy is diagnosed by voltage criteria, and 520 ms is abnormal in either sex.

quiz.q: Lead I is predominantly upright and lead aVF is predominantly negative. What is the axis?
choices: Right axis deviation
Extreme axis deviation
Normal axis
Left axis deviation
quiz.why: Upright in I with a negative aVF places the vector between -30 and -90 degrees, which is left axis deviation. Both upright is normal, I negative with aVF upright is right axis deviation, and both negative is the extreme quadrant.

quiz.q: Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows FEV1 2.20 L (66 percent predicted), FVC 3.20 L, and FEV1/FVC 0.69. How is this classified?
choices: Normal spirometry
Moderate obstruction, since the ratio is below 0.70 and the FEV1 falls in the 50 to 79 percent band
Restriction, since the FEV1 is reduced
Severe obstruction requiring immediate hospitalization
quiz.why: A post-bronchodilator ratio under 0.70 defines obstruction, and severity is then graded on FEV1 percent predicted, placing 66 percent in the moderate band of 50 to 79. Restriction would show a normal or high ratio, and severe disease begins under 50 percent.

quiz.q: A bronchodilator raises a patient's FEV1 from 1.50 L to 1.74 L. Is this a significant response and what does it suggest?
choices: No, because the absolute change is under 200 mL
Yes, because the change is 16 percent AND 240 mL, which points toward asthma
Yes, because any improvement is significant
No, because reversibility testing requires a 25 percent change
quiz.why: The threshold is at least 12 percent and at least 200 mL, and 240 mL is a 16 percent rise, meeting both and favoring asthma over COPD. The absolute change does exceed 200 mL, and neither any-improvement nor a 25 percent threshold is the standard.

quiz.q: Why can spirometry alone never confirm a restrictive defect?
choices: Restriction is defined by the FEV1/FVC ratio, which spirometry measures poorly
Restrictive disease does not change any spirometric value
Spirometry does not measure FVC
A low FVC can also be produced by poor effort or by severe air trapping, so total lung capacity below 80 percent predicted is required
quiz.why: Spirometry cannot measure residual volume, so a reduced FVC may reflect trapped gas or submaximal effort rather than small lungs; plethysmography or gas dilution gives the total lung capacity that defines restriction. Spirometry does measure FVC and the ratio reliably.

quiz.q: An intubated patient has a peak pressure of 44 and a plateau pressure of 21 cm H2O. What is the problem and what is the first action?
choices: A resistance problem; suction the tube and check for bronchospasm, a kink or biting
A leak; check the cuff
Normal pressures; no action needed
A compliance problem; obtain an urgent chest x-ray for pneumothorax
quiz.why: A high peak with a normal plateau localizes the problem to resistance in the circuit or airways, so suctioning, checking for a kink or bite and treating bronchospasm come first. A compliance problem raises both pressures, and a leak lowers pressures rather than raising them.

quiz.q: A 6-foot man with a predicted body weight of about 80 kg is intubated for septic shock without ARDS. Which initial tidal volume is appropriate?
choices: Set by actual weight of 110 kg at 8 mL/kg
480 to 640 mL
300 mL
quiz.why: Tidal volume is 6 to 8 mL/kg of predicted body weight calculated from height, giving roughly 480 to 640 mL for an 80 kg predicted weight. Using actual weight in an obese patient overdistends lungs that did not grow with the body, and 1200 mL and 300 mL fall far outside the range.

quiz.q: A ventilated patient has a plateau pressure of 34 cm H2O on a PEEP of 8. What are the plateau and driving pressures telling you?
choices: The driving pressure is 34 and is the only number that matters
PEEP should be increased to lower the plateau
Both are acceptable and no change is needed
The plateau exceeds 30 and the driving pressure of 26 exceeds about 15, so the tidal volume should be reduced
quiz.why: Plateau should stay under 30 cm H2O and driving pressure, plateau minus PEEP, under about 15, and 34 with a driving pressure of 26 breaches both, so tidal volume comes down. Raising PEEP raises plateau further rather than protecting the lung.

quiz.q: Pleural fluid returns with a protein ratio of 0.31, an LDH ratio of 0.44, and a pleural LDH of 120 with a serum upper limit of 250. Which underlying process fits best?
choices: Malignant pleural disease
A transudate from heart failure, cirrhosis or nephrotic syndrome
Tuberculous pleuritis
Empyema requiring a chest tube
quiz.why: None of Light's criteria are met, so the fluid is a transudate, meaning healthy pleura with a pressure or oncotic problem. Empyema, malignancy and tuberculosis are all exudative processes that would breach at least one criterion.

quiz.q: During thoracentesis for a chronic effusion, 1.6 L has been drained and the patient begins coughing and desaturating. What has most likely happened?
choices: An air embolism from the drainage tubing
Hypovolemia from protein loss in the drained fluid
Re-expansion pulmonary edema from draining a chronically collapsed lung too quickly
A new empyema
quiz.why: Removing more than about 1.5 L at once can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema, presenting exactly as cough and hypoxemia during or just after the procedure. Empyema and protein loss do not occur within minutes, and air embolism is rare and would not follow simple over-drainage.

quiz.q: A tall, thin 20-year-old smoker has a small primary spontaneous pneumothorax and stable vital signs. Roughly how fast does trapped air resorb on room air, and what changes that?
choices: About 1 to 2 percent per day; high-flow oxygen speeds it several times over by washing out nitrogen
It never resorbs without a chest tube
About 1 to 2 percent per day; oxygen slows resorption
About 10 percent of the hemithorax per day; oxygen makes no difference
quiz.why: Air resorbs at roughly 1 to 2 percent of the hemithorax daily, and high-flow oxygen lowers blood nitrogen and steepens the gradient pulling trapped nitrogen out, accelerating it several-fold. Small stable primary pneumothoraces frequently resolve without a tube.

quiz.q: Which value now defines pulmonary hypertension at rest?
choices: A mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg
A systolic pulmonary artery pressure above 40 mmHg
A mean pulmonary artery pressure above 35 mmHg
A pulmonary capillary wedge pressure above 25 mmHg
quiz.why: The threshold is a mean pulmonary artery pressure above 20 mmHg, lowered from the older 25 mmHg cutoff. Wedge pressure is used to separate pre- from post-capillary disease rather than to define pulmonary hypertension, and the definition uses mean rather than systolic pressure.

quiz.q: Why does systemic hypotension in right ventricular failure become self-perpetuating?
choices: The left ventricle steals coronary flow from the right
Hypotension triggers a vagal reflex that stops the heart
The right ventricle normally perfuses in both systole and diastole, so a falling systemic pressure starves it and worsens its failure
Hypotension causes immediate pulmonary vasodilation
quiz.why: Right coronary flow normally continues through systole because right ventricular pressure is low, but in failure the wall tension rises and flow depends on systemic pressure, so hypotension causes right ventricular ischemia and further failure. There is no coronary steal or reflex arrest driving this loop.

quiz.q: A patient with known pulmonary hypertension has jugular venous distension, a parasternal heave, a loud P2, a murmur at the lower sternal border that increases with inspiration, and a pulsatile liver. What is the diagnosis?
choices: Left-sided heart failure
Cor pulmonale with tricuspid regurgitation
Aortic stenosis
Constrictive pericarditis alone
quiz.why: Every finding listed is right-sided: a heave, a loud P2, an inspiration-augmented tricuspid murmur and a pulsatile liver define right heart failure from lung disease. Left heart failure gives pulmonary crackles and an S3 at the apex, and aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids.

quiz.q: A 2-week-old has a harsh holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, poor weight gain, and tachypnea with feeds, but is pink with a saturation of 98 percent. Which lesion fits and why is he not cyanotic?
choices: Tetralogy of Fallot; the pulmonic stenosis is mild
Transposition of the great arteries; a large ductus is mixing blood
Coarctation of the aorta; the murmur is from the narrowed segment
Ventricular septal defect; the shunt is left to right, so pulmonary flow is excessive but systemic blood stays oxygenated
quiz.why: A harsh holosystolic murmur at the lower sternal border with pulmonary overcirculation and failure to thrive is a ventricular septal defect, an acyanotic left-to-right shunt. Tetralogy and transposition cause cyanosis, and coarctation produces upper extremity hypertension with weak femoral pulses.

quiz.q: A neonate is started on prostaglandin E1 for a suspected ductal-dependent lesion. Which side effect must you be prepared for?
choices: Immediate ductal closure
Severe hypertension
Apnea
Hyperkalemia
quiz.why: Apnea is the characteristic adverse effect of prostaglandin E1, so airway support must be immediately available. The drug keeps the ductus open rather than closing it, and hypertension and hyperkalemia are not its typical effects.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old with an unrepaired atrial septal defect is now cyanotic with clubbing and a pulmonary vascular resistance exceeding systemic. What has happened and what is now contraindicated?
choices: Eisenmenger syndrome has developed; closing the defect is contraindicated
A new ventricular septal defect has formed; closure is urgent
Tetralogy of Fallot has developed; a tet spell is imminent
The defect has closed spontaneously; anticoagulation is contraindicated
quiz.why: Years of left-to-right shunting remodel the pulmonary vasculature until resistance exceeds systemic and the shunt reverses, which is Eisenmenger syndrome; the defect is then the only relief valve for the right ventricle and must not be closed. Tetralogy is congenital rather than acquired, and the defect has not closed.

quiz.q: A climber at 14,000 feet develops ataxia and confusion 36 hours after ascent. What is the syndrome and the single most important treatment?
choices: Hypoglycemia; oral glucose
Acute mountain sickness; acetazolamide and rest at altitude
High altitude pulmonary edema; nifedipine at altitude
High altitude cerebral edema; immediate descent, plus dexamethasone and oxygen
quiz.why: Ataxia with altered mental status at altitude is cerebral edema, and descent is the treatment that saves the patient, with dexamethasone and oxygen as adjuncts. Acute mountain sickness is headache with nausea or insomnia without neurologic signs, and pulmonary edema presents with dyspnea and hypoxemia.

quiz.q: Why does the greatest proportional gas volume change during diving occur in the shallowest water?
choices: Because nitrogen dissolves fastest near the surface
Because Boyle's law makes the first 33 feet a doubling or halving of absolute pressure, the largest relative change
Because water temperature changes most near the surface
Because oxygen becomes toxic above 33 feet
quiz.why: Pressure rises one atmosphere per 33 feet, so descending from 1 to 2 atmospheres halves gas volume, a far larger proportional change than any deeper 33-foot increment, which is why breath-hold ascent from shallow depth ruptures alveoli. Nitrogen loading under Henry's law explains decompression sickness, not barotrauma.

quiz.q: A chronic smoker has a resting carboxyhemoglobin of 7 percent. Which consequence follows directly from this?
choices: A falsely low SpO2 reading
An SpO2 reading that may overestimate true oxygen saturation because the oximeter cannot distinguish carboxyhemoglobin
A right shift of the oxyhemoglobin curve improving tissue delivery
An increased number of available hemoglobin binding sites
quiz.why: A standard pulse oximeter reads carboxyhemoglobin as if it were oxyhemoglobin, so the displayed saturation runs high; co-oximetry is needed to separate them. Carbon monoxide shifts the curve left and occupies binding sites rather than adding them.
